---

**Card 5 — Easy mode**
- **Plain name:** The too-polite problem
- **One-liner:** When a simulator is too agreeable — approving too much and rarely pushing back — so the coding agent it tests looks better than real users would ever let it.
- **Why it matters:** The whole point of a user simulator is to stress-test a coding agent the way a real, sometimes-annoyed developer would. A too-polite simulator removes the friction — the bug reports, interruptions, pushback — and quietly grades the agent on a curve. An agent that passes against an easy-mode simulator may still frustrate real developers. This is the headline failure of every live model tested.

**Plain-English note under the table:**

No single column names a winner: the highest CondAgree is with-profile Gemini (0.333) — genuine situational skill, ≈2× the 0.163 lucky-guess line — yet it approves 72.2%. Color semantics site-wide: **emerald** = at/near real or clearly above the lucky-guess line (good); **amber** = easy-mode / threshold / caution; **blue** = live frontier model (neutral); **zinc** = reference rows + tracks. 1. Hero stat + mini-bar *(spec in §1)*
2. Metric primer cards *(spec in §3)*
3. Move-mix comparison: Real vs. simulators (centerpiece)
4. Leaderboard table *(spec in §4)*
5. The dumb-sampler trap (MoveFid × CondAgree scatter)
6. The persona-profile lift (with-profile vs. no-profile dumbbells)
7. The transfer story (3 model callouts)
8. Caveats footer *(spec in §6)*

**VISUAL A — Move-mix comparison: Real vs. simulators (centerpiece)**

Two stacked sub-panels: **APPROVE%** and **CRITICAL%**. Each panel has 8 horizontal bars (6 live runs + 2 references), scale 0–100%, with a dashed emerald vertical baseline.

| Row | Value | Bar color |
|---|---|---|
| deepseek · with-profile | 42.6% | blue |
| deepseek · no-profile | 49.1% | blue |
| gpt-5 · with-profile | 38.9% | blue |
| gpt-5 · no-profile | 24.5% | emerald (≈ baseline; flag "best-calibrated, no-profile only") |
| gemini · with-profile | 72.2% | amber (worst offender) |
| gemini · no-profile | 66.7% | amber |

*CRITICAL% panel — baseline dashed line at 33% ("real 33%"):*

| Row | Value | Bar color |
|---|---|---|
| deepseek · with-profile | 9.3% | amber |
| deepseek · no-profile | 5.7% | amber |
| gpt-5 · with-profile | 3.7% | amber |

| gemini · with-profile | 3.7% | amber |

On critical%, every live model falls *short* of 33%, clustering at 3.7–11.3%. Only the dumb `prior_sampler` reaches the real critical rate (35.2%), and only `always_approve` hits 100% approve. *Points (x = MoveFid, y = CondAgree):*
- deepseek · with-profile (53.9, 0.315) — blue
- deepseek · no-profile (39.8, 0.189) — blue, just above line
- gpt-5 · with-profile (45.5, 0.278) — blue
- gpt-5 · no-profile (52.4, 0.189) — blue, just above line
- gemini · with-profile (41.4, 0.333) — blue, highest dot; label "≈2× the line"
- gemini · no-profile (49.0, 0.278) — blue

**VISUAL C — The persona-profile lift (dumbbells)**

Three slim dumbbell rows, one per model, on a 0–0.40 CondAgree axis. Hollow dot = no-profile, filled dot = with-profile, connector line between, `+delta` labeled trailing. A small amber sub-note per row shows the approve% side-effect.

*CondAgree (no-profile → with-profile, delta):*
- deepseek-v3.1: 0.189 → 0.315, **+0.126** (emerald; biggest gain — "most coachable")
- gpt-5: 0.189 → 0.278, **+0.089** (emerald)
- gemini-3.1-pro: 0.278 → 0.333, **+0.055** (emerald)

*approve% side-effect (no-profile → with-profile), amber sub-note:*
- deepseek: 49.1% → 42.6% (down — improves)
- gpt-5: 24.5% → 38.9% (**up** — approves more; amber)
- gemini: 66.7% → 72.2% (**up** — approves more; amber)

**Caption:** Giving the simulator a profile of the specific developer raises right-move-right-place for all three (DeepSeek gains most, +0.126). But it doesn't cure easy mode: for GPT-5 and Gemini the profile makes them approve *even more* (24.5→38.9%, 66.7→72.2%). With one run per cell, read the direction, not the exact ordering of the deltas.

---

**VISUAL D — The transfer story (3 callout cards)**

Three equal text-forward cards, each: prior-work chip → what happened here, with one highlighted numeral.

- **DeepSeek-V3.1** — chip `prior work: best simulator (USI 76.0)`. Here: "the most **coachable** — biggest profile gain (**+0.126**) and top with-profile MoveFid (**53.9**)." Tone: emerald.
- **GPT-5** — chip `prior work: strong, not best (USI ~70.9)`. Here: "best-calibrated approve rate with no profile (**24.5%** ≈ real 24%) — yet still barely pushes back (critical **11.3%**)." Tone: blue/amber.
- **Gemini-3.1-Pro** — chip `prior work: most human-like`. Here: "the **worst** easy-mode offender — approves **72.2%**, ~3× real. Sounding human ≠ behaving like a developer." Tone: amber.

**Caption (full-width below):** USI was the combined quality score from prior customer-service-simulator research. Today's top models are too polite to stand in for real developers. Being good at *sounding human*, or at *simulating customers*, does not make a good *coder* simulator.

---

## 6. CAVEATS

Render as one muted line (zinc-500, small) in the footer, and echo a one-line version beside the leaderboard ("One generation per cell — treat small row-to-row gaps as noise; the easy-mode pattern is the robust signal.").

> **Caveats.** This rests on 54 moments from 9 users, with one generation per cell (so no error bars — treat tiny gaps as noise), moves labeled by a single AI classifier (claude-haiku-4.5, whose errors bound every number), percentages that exclude the small "other" move category and so may not sum to exactly 100%, and a **request-side** setup — we held the real coding agent fixed and asked for the developer's next message, rather than letting the simulator drive a live agent and measuring task outcomes. The easy-mode effect, though, is large and consistent across every live model.

cd /Users/kevin/Dev/user-simulator
pkill -f "http.server 8799" 2>/dev/null
git add -A
echo "=== staged changes ==="; git status --short
git commit -q -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
Rebuild site: UserSimBench v0 results (replaces trace viewer)

Old trace-viewer/analysis site preserved on branch
backup/trace-viewer-pre-usersimbench.

New single-page site presents the v0 move-fidelity findings for a reader
who knows SWE-chat but is new to user simulation: every frontier model is
"easy mode" (approves 39-72% vs real 24%, critical only 3.7-11.3% vs real
33%); MoveFid alone is gameable (dumb prior_sampler tops it at 84.3); the
distilled profile lifts CondAgree but not easy-mode; transfer from prior
work is selective (DeepSeek coachable, GPT-5 calibrated, Gemini worst).

Metrics rewritten for accessibility (no scary formulas): MoveFid =
"right-mix score", CondAgree = "right-move-right-place", Sigma p^2 =
"the lucky-guess line (0.163)". Plain-English metric cards, real-vs-sim
approve/critical bars, MoveFid x CondAgree scatter, persona-lift
dumbbells, transfer cards. Data in public/data/v0_results.json.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.REDACTED
EOF
)"

"""vLLM OpenAI-compatible inference server on Modal.

Serves the merged user-sim model behind a public URL. Drop-in for `with-user`:
  export OPENAI_API_BASE="https://<your-url>/v1"
  export OPENAI_API_KEY="<token>"
  --user-model openai/user-sim
"""
import os
import subprocess
import time

import modal

from common import app, serve_image, volume, VOL_MOUNT, CKPT_DIR


SERVED_MODEL_NAME = "user-sim"  # MUST NOT contain anthropic/claude/sonnet/opus/haiku
API_KEY_PLACEHOLDER = "user-sim-dev-key"  # for prod, mount as Secret


@app.function(
    image=serve_image,
    # L40S has 48GB which fits Qwen3-8B bf16 + KV cache easily, at ~$1.95/h
    # (vs A100-80GB at $2.50/h). For higher throughput swap to "A100-80GB".
    gpu="L40S",
    volumes={VOL_MOUNT: volume},
    secrets=[modal.Secret.from_name("huggingface")],
    timeout=60 * 60 * 4,
    scaledown_window=60 * 5,
    max_containers=1,
)
@modal.concurrent(max_inputs=64)
@modal.web_server(port=8000, startup_timeout=600)
def serve():
    run_name = os.environ.get("USER_SIM_RUN_NAME", "qwen25-7b-marcus-sa-v1")
    model_dir = f"{CKPT_DIR}/{run_name}/merged"
    print(f"[serve] starting vLLM with model_dir={model_dir} served_name={SERVED_MODEL_NAME}")

    cmd = [
        "python", "-m", "vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server",
        "--model", model_dir,
        "--served-model-name", SERVED_MODEL_NAME,
        "--port", "8000",
        "--host", "0.0.0.0",
        "--api-key", os.environ.get("USER_SIM_API_KEY", API_KEY_PLACEHOLDER),
        "--max-model-len", "16384",
        "--gpu-memory-utilization", "0.92",
        "--dtype", "bfloat16",
        "--enable-prefix-caching",
    ]
    print("[serve] cmd:", " ".join(cmd))
    subprocess.Popen(cmd)


@app.local_entrypoint()
def main():
    """Deploy via `modal deploy serve.py` instead of running this.

    `modal run serve.py` would invoke `main` synchronously rather than
    starting the web server."""
    print(

"""Shared Modal config: app, image, volume."""
import modal

APP_NAME = "user-sim-marcus-sa"

# Volume V2 for heavy storage: HF cache, processed datasets, model checkpoints.
volume = modal.Volume.from_name("user-sim-vol", version=2, create_if_missing=True)
VOL_MOUNT = "/vol"

HF_CACHE = f"{VOL_MOUNT}/hf_cache"
DATA_DIR = f"{VOL_MOUNT}/data"
CKPT_DIR = f"{VOL_MOUNT}/ckpt"

# Base image for data prep (light)
data_image = (
    modal.Image.debian_slim(python_version="3.11")
    .pip_install(
        "datasets==4.4.1",
        "huggingface_hub==0.36.0",
        "pandas==2.2.3",
        "pyarrow==21.0.0",
        "jinja2==3.1.6",
    )
    .env({"HF_HOME": HF_CACHE})
    .add_local_python_source("common")
)

# Heavy image for training: CUDA + torch + trl + peft (Qwen3.5 needs newer transformers)
train_image = (
    modal.Image.from_registry("nvidia/cuda:12.4.1-cudnn-devel-ubuntu22.04", add_python="3.11")
    .apt_install("git", "build-essential")
    .pip_install(
        "torch==2.5.1",
        # Qwen3.5 (model_type=qwen3_5) is newer than any tagged transformers
        # release; install from main and let pip resolve compatible versions
        # of the surrounding stack.
        "transformers @ git+https://github.com/huggingface/transformers.git@main",
        "accelerate",
        "peft",
        "trl",
        "datasets",
        "bitsandbytes",
        "huggingface_hub",
        "tensorboard",
        "sentencepiece",
        "tiktoken",
        "protobuf",
        # Memory-efficient kernels (chunked cross-entropy, fused RMSNorm, etc.)
        # so we can train Qwen3.5 at seq 32K within H100-80GB.
        "liger-kernel",
        # FlashAttention 2 -- essential for sub-O(L^2) attention at seq 32K.
        # Without it Qwen3.5's SDPA falls back to math kernel = ~10x slower.
        "ninja", "packaging", "wheel",
    )
    # flash-attn needs torch installed first (it builds against torch headers)
    # so we put it in a separate pip_install call after the main stack.
    .pip_install("flash-attn", extra_options="--no-build-isolation")
    .env({"HF_HOME": HF_CACHE, "TOKENIZERS_PARALLELISM": "false"})
    .add_local_python_source("common")
)

# OSim-8B (post-trained, text)

**OSim-8B** is the post-trained (text) checkpoint of **OSim** (OdysSim), a foundation model for **human behavior simulation** — trained to imitate the *human / user* side of interactions rather than to behave as a helpful assistant. It is the text counterpart of the midtrained [`cmu-lti/osim-8b-mid`](https://huggingface.co/cmu-lti/osim-8b-mid): [`Qwen/Qwen3-8B`](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-8B) midtrained on the OdysSim corpus (62 behavioral datasets along the five **Soul** axes — CONV/SS/COG/ROLE/EVAL) and then post-trained (task-specific RL + expert consolidation).

*(Mirror of `sunweiwei/OSim-8B`, the text post model. For the VL variant see `sunweiwei/OSim-Inst-8B`.)*

## Intended use

Simulating the human/user side of conversations — user simulation for agent evaluation, social simulation, persona / role-play. Conditioned on a "social-context" system prompt (who is speaking: role, goal, background, style); given the other party's turns it generates the next human turn.

## Results

Evaluated **out-of-distribution** as the user simulator in the τ-USI agentic benchmark (τ-bench airline+retail, 165 tasks, fixed GPT-5.2 agent), OSim-8B reaches **USI 75.6** — the **best behavioral / specialized user simulator**, surpassing same-size general instruct models and every prior specialized simulator (CoSER-8B 67.2, UserLM-8B 62.0). It is distinctively human-like in **reactivity** (Sørensen–Dice D4 ≈ 93, matching the human inter-annotator level) and in **outcome calibration** (best ECE among compared models), with essentially none of the long-horizon agentic failure modes (timeouts/perseveration) seen in non-behavioral baselines.

## Training

- **Base:** Qwen3-8B
- **Stages:** midtraining on the OdysSim corpus → task-specific reinforcement learning + expert consolidation.

## Citation

If you use this model, please cite the OdysSim paper (*Building Foundation Models for Human Behavior Simulation*). Code: https://github.com/sunnweiwei/OdysSim

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""OpenAI-compatible client for the OSim (OdysSim) vLLM endpoints on Modal, plus
the model's NATIVE role-swapped prompt format.

OSim plays the human/user side: it is conditioned on a social-context system prompt
(who the developer is) and the *other party's* (coding agent's) turns, and generates
the next human (developer) turn. In a chat template the generated role is "assistant",
so we swap: agent turns -> role "user", the developer's own prior turns -> "assistant".
"""
import json
import re
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.request

# filled in by the runner once `modal deploy` prints the URLs
ENDPOINTS = {
    "osim-8b": "https://kevinli020508--osim-eval-serve-8b.modal.run/v1",
    "osim-4b": "https://kevinli020508--osim-eval-serve-4b.modal.run/v1",
}
API_KEY = "osim-eval-key"

_THINK = re.compile(r"<think>.*?</think>", re.S)


def _clean(t: str) -> str:
    s = _THINK.sub("", t or "").strip()
    for tag in ("DEVELOPER:", "USER:", "Developer:", "User:", "Message:"):
        if s.startswith(tag):
            s = s[len(tag):].strip()
    if len(s) >= 2 and s[0] == s[-1] and s[0] in "\"'":
        s = s[1:-1].strip()
    return s


def build_osim_messages(point, folder_text, truncate_words, context_turn_words=200):
    """Role-swapped messages: system = social context (the developer persona),
    then the conversation with agent='user' and developer='assistant'. Consecutive
    same-role turns are merged so the chat template stays well-formed."""
    if folder_text:
        system = (
            "You are role-playing a specific real software developer who is using an AI "
            "coding agent. The profile below is who you are — your background, voice, "
            "preferences and how you drive a coding session.\n\n"
            f"{folder_text}\n\n"
            "Continue as this developer: read what the agent just did and write your next "
            "message to it, exactly as this developer would type it (their length, casing, "
            "typos and idiom). Output only the message."
        )
    else:
        system = (
            "You are role-playing a software developer using an AI coding agent. Read what "
            "the agent just did and write your next message to it — the move you would "
            "actually make (often new work, a redirect, a question, or a problem you "
            "noticed, not just approval). Output only the message."
        )
    # swap roles: SWE-chat user(=developer) -> assistant ; assistant(=agent) -> user
    swapped = []
    for t in point["context"]:
        role = "assistant" if t["role"] == "user" else "user"
        swapped.append({"role": role, "content": truncate_words(t["text"], context_turn_words)})
    # merge consecutive same-role
    merged = []
    for m in swapped:
        if merged and merged[-1]["role"] == m["role"]:
            merged[-1]["content"] += "\n\n" + m["content"]
        else:
            merged.append(dict(m))

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""OpenAI-compatible client for the OSim (OdysSim) vLLM endpoints on Modal, plus
the model's NATIVE role-swapped prompt format.

OSim plays the human/user side: it is conditioned on a social-context system prompt
(who the developer is) and the *other party's* (coding agent's) turns, and generates
the next human (developer) turn. In a chat template the generated role is "assistant",
so we swap: agent turns -> role "user", the developer's own prior turns -> "assistant".
"""
import json
import re
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.request

# filled in by the runner once `modal deploy` prints the URLs
ENDPOINTS = {
    "osim-8b": "https://kevinli020508--osim-eval-serve-8b.modal.run/v1",
    "osim-4b": "https://kevinli020508--osim-eval-serve-4b.modal.run/v1",
}
API_KEY = "osim-eval-key"

_THINK = re.compile(r"<think>.*?</think>", re.S)


def _clean(t: str) -> str:
    s = _THINK.sub("", t or "").strip()
    for tag in ("DEVELOPER:", "USER:", "Developer:", "User:", "Message:"):
        if s.startswith(tag):
            s = s[len(tag):].strip()
    if len(s) >= 2 and s[0] == s[-1] and s[0] in "\"'":
        s = s[1:-1].strip()
    return s


def build_osim_messages(point, folder_text, truncate_words, context_turn_words=200):
    """Role-swapped messages: system = social context (the developer persona),
    then the conversation with agent='user' and developer='assistant'. Consecutive
    same-role turns are merged so the chat template stays well-formed."""
    if folder_text:
        system = (
            "You are role-playing a specific real software developer who is using an AI "
            "coding agent. The profile below is who you are — your background, voice, "
            "preferences and how you drive a coding session.\n\n"
            f"{folder_text}\n\n"
            "Continue as this developer: read what the agent just did and write your next "
            "message to it, exactly as this developer would type it (their length, casing, "
            "typos and idiom). Output only the message."
        )
    else:
        system = (
            "You are role-playing a software developer using an AI coding agent. Read what "
            "the agent just did and write your next message to it — the move you would "
            "actually make (often new work, a redirect, a question, or a problem you "
            "noticed, not just approval). Output only the message."
        )
    # swap roles: SWE-chat user(=developer) -> assistant ; assistant(=agent) -> user
    swapped = []
    for t in point["context"]:
        role = "assistant" if t["role"] == "user" else "user"
        swapped.append({"role": role, "content": truncate_words(t["text"], context_turn_words)})
    # merge consecutive same-role
    merged = []
    for m in swapped:
        if merged and merged[-1]["role"] == m["role"]:
            merged[-1]["content"] += "\n\n" + m["content"]
        else:

    # message should be a "user" (agent) turn; if not, append a nudge.
    if not merged or merged[-1]["role"] != "user":

    return [{"role": "system", "content": system}] + merged

        "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False},
    }
    data = json.dumps(body).encode()
    last = ""
    for attempt in range(retries):
        try:
            req = urllib.request.Request(
                base_url.rstrip("/") + "/chat/completions", data=data,
                headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}", "Content-Type": "application/json"})
            with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=timeout) as r:
                d = json.loads(r.read())

            if ch:
                c = _clean(ch[0].get("message", {}).get("content") or "")
                if c:
                    return c
            last = json.dumps(d.get("error") or {"empty": True})[:200]
        except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
            try:
                last = f"HTTP {e.code}: {e.read().decode()[:200]}"
            except Exception:
                last = f"HTTP {e.code}"
        except Exception as e:  # noqa: BLE001
            last = f"{type(e).__name__}: {str(e)[:200]}"

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Run the OdysSim OSim-4B / OSim-8B simulators through the v0 move-fidelity eval
(same 54 points, same move classifier, same metrics) and merge into the leaderboard.

OSim uses its native role-swapped format (bench/osim_backend.py). Reuses everything
else from v0.py so the numbers are directly comparable to the frontier models.

Usage: python3 bench/v0_osim.py [--limit N]
"""
import argparse
import json
import sys
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT / "scripts"))
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT / "bench"))
import validate as V          # noqa: E402
import v0                     # noqa: E402  (load_points, classify_move, score_block, dist, ...)
import osim_backend as OB     # noqa: E402

RESULTS = ROOT / "bench" / "results"
RAW = RESULTS / "v0_osim_raw.jsonl"
FRONTIER_RAW = RESULTS / "v0_raw.jsonl"
COMBINED = RESULTS / "v0_with_osim_summary.json"
MODELS = ["osim-8b", "osim-4b"]
CONDS = ["distilled", "generic"]


def load_cache(path):
    c = {}
    if path.exists():
        for line in path.read_text().splitlines():
            if line.strip():
                r = json.loads(line)
                c[r["key"]] = r
    return c


def append(path, rec):
    with path.open("a") as f:
        f.write(json.dumps(rec, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--limit", type=int, default=0)
    args = ap.parse_args()

    points = v0.load_points()
    if args.limit:
        points = points[:args.limit]
    by_id = {p["point_id"]: p for p in points}
    print(f"{len(points)} points")

    # real move labels: reuse the frontier run's labels for identical ground truth
    fcache = load_cache(FRONTIER_RAW)
    real_move = {pid: fcache.get(f"label|real|{pid}", {}).get("move") for pid in by_id}
    missing_real = [pid for pid in by_id if not real_move[pid]]
    if missing_real:
        print(f"labeling {len(missing_real)} missing real moves...")
        with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=8) as ex:
            futs = {ex.submit(v0.classify_move, by_id[pid]["real"], by_id[pid]["prev_agent"]): pid for pid in missing_real}
            for fut in as_completed(futs):
                real_move[futs[fut]] = fut.result()

    cache = load_cache(RAW)

    # 1. generate (OSim native format)
    gen_jobs = [(p, m, c) for p in points for m in MODELS for c in CONDS
                if f"gen|{p['point_id']}|{m}|{c}" not in cache]
    print(f"generations to run: {len(gen_jobs)}")

    def run_gen(job):
        p, m, c = job
        folder = V.load_folder_text(p["slug"]) if c == "distilled" else ""
        msgs = OB.build_osim_messages(p, folder, V.truncate_words)
        txt = OB.chat(m, msgs)
        return {"key": f"gen|{p['point_id']}|{m}|{c}", "kind": "gen",
                "point_id": p["point_id"], "slug": p["slug"], "model": m, "cond": c, "text": txt}

    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=6) as ex:
        for i, fut in enumerate(as_completed([ex.submit(run_gen, j) for j in gen_jobs]), 1):
            rec = fut.result(); cache[rec["key"]] = rec; append(RAW, rec)
            if i % 20 == 0:
                print(f"  gen {i}/{len(gen_jobs)}")

    # 2. label moves
    lab_jobs = []
    for p in points:
        for m in MODELS:
            for c in CONDS:
                g = cache.get(f"gen|{p['point_id']}|{m}|{c}")
                lk = f"label|{m}|{c}|{p['point_id']}"
                if g and lk not in cache:
                    lab_jobs.append((lk, g["text"], p["prev_agent"]))
    print(f"labels to run: {len(lab_jobs)}")

    def run_lab(job):
        lk, text, prev = job
        return {"key": lk, "kind": "label", "move": v0.classify_move(text, prev)}

    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=8) as ex:
        for i, fut in enumerate(as_completed([ex.submit(run_lab, j) for j in lab_jobs]), 1):
            rec = fut.result(); cache[rec["key"]] = rec; append(RAW, rec)
            if i % 30 == 0:
                print(f"  label {i}/{len(lab_jobs)}")

    # 3. metrics (same machinery as v0)
    valid = [pid for pid in by_id if real_move[pid]]
    real_moves = [real_move[pid] for pid in valid]
    osim_results = {}
    for m in MODELS:
        for c in CONDS:
            sim, paired = [], []
            for pid in valid:
                sm = cache.get(f"label|{m}|{c}|{pid}", {}).get("move")
                gt = cache.get(f"gen|{pid}|{m}|{c}", {})
                if sm and not V.is_cli_failure(gt.get("text", "")):
                    sim.append(sm); paired.append((real_move[pid], sm))
            osim_results[f"{m}/{c}"] = v0.score_block(real_moves, sim, paired)

    # 4. merge with frontier summary + print combined leaderboard
    front = json.loads((RESULTS / "v0_summary.json").read_text())
    combined = dict(front)
    combined["results"] = {**front["results"], **osim_results}
    COMBINED.write_text(json.dumps(combined, indent=1, ensure_ascii=False))

    real_appr, real_crit = front["real_approve%"], front["real_critical%"]
    ceil = front["condagree_marginal_ceiling"]
    print(f"\nreal: approve%={real_appr} critical%={real_crit}  Σp²={ceil}\n")
    hdr = f"{'simulator':26s} {'MoveFid':>7} {'CondAgr':>7} {'appr%':>6} {'crit%':>6} {'n':>4}"
    print(hdr); print("-" * len(hdr))
    order = ([f"{m}/{c}" for m in MODELS for c in CONDS] +
             ["deepseek-v3.1/distilled", "gpt-5/distilled", "gemini-3.1-pro/distilled",
              "deepseek-v3.1/generic", "gpt-5/generic", "gemini-3.1-pro/generic",
              "[ref] prior_sampler"])
    for k in order:
        r = combined["results"].get(k)
        if not r:
            continue
        tag = "  <- OSim" if k.startswith("osim") else ""
        print(f"{k:26s} {str(r['MoveFid']):>7} {str(r['CondAgree']):>7} "
              f"{str(r['approve%']):>6} {str(r['critical%']):>6} {r['n']:>4}{tag}")
    print(f"\nwrote {COMBINED}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

#!/bin/bash

  [ "${ready[8b]}" = "1" ] && [ "${ready[4b]}" = "1" ] && { echo "BOTH READY"; break; }

done
echo "=== /v1/models responses ==="
for m in 8b 4b; do echo "--$m--"; head -c 300 /tmp/osim_$m.json; echo; done
EOF
chmod +x /tmp/warm_osim.sh
bash /tmp/warm_osim.sh > /tmp/warm_osim.log 2>&1
echo "warm exit=$?"; tail -8 /tmp/warm_osim.log

input.content:
# UserSimBench v0 — OdysSim (OSim) add-on findings

**Question.** OSim-8B was the **best specialized user simulator in prior work** (τ-USI 75.6, with
near-human reactivity D4≈93 on customer-service τ-bench). Does that specialization *transfer* to
driving a coding agent — i.e., is the purpose-built user-sim less "easy mode" than the frontier
models?

**Setup.** Hosted `cmu-lti/osim-8b` and `cmu-lti/osim-4b` (Qwen3-8B/4B, MIT) on Modal via vLLM
(OpenAI-compatible), using OSim's **native role-swapped format** (system = developer social-context
/ persona; the agent's turns as input; the model generates the next *developer* turn). Same 54
held-out points, same move classifier, same metrics as the frontier run.

## Leaderboard (OSim vs frontier)

Real developers: approve **24%**, critical **33%**; lucky-guess line (Σp²) **0.163**.

| simulator | MoveFid↑ | CondAgree↑ | approve% (24) | critical% (33) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **osim-8b** / generic | **56.5** | 0.208 | 9.4% | 9.4% |
| **osim-8b** / distilled | 55.8 | 0.222 | 42.6% | **16.7%** |
| osim-4b / generic | 55.1 | 0.111 | 24.1% | 11.1% |
| osim-4b / distilled | 48.7 | 0.259 | 57.4% | 13.0% |
| deepseek-v3.1 / distilled | 53.9 | 0.315 | 42.6% | 9.3% |
| gpt-5 / distilled | 45.5 | 0.278 | 38.9% | 3.7% |
| gemini-3.1-pro / distilled | 41.4 | **0.333** | 72.2% | 3.7% |
| gpt-5 / generic | 52.4 | 0.189 | 24.5% | 11.3% |
| _[ref] prior_sampler_ | _84.3_ | _0.185_ | _20.4%_ | _35.2%_ |

## Findings

**1. The specialized simulator wins move-mix fidelity.** OSim-8B tops every live model on MoveFid
(56.5 / 55.8) — its training objective (match the *distribution* of human behavior) transfers
directly. It produces the most realistic overall *blend* of moves.

**2. OSim is the least "easy mode" — its anti-sycophancy partially transfers.** OSim-8B/distilled is
**critical 16.7%** — the highest of any live model, ~½ of the real 33% rate, vs the frontier models'
3.7–11.3%. And OSim-8B doesn't over-approve: generic it approves just **9.4%** (it *asks questions*
40% of the time instead). So the human-like reactivity OSim was trained for (D4≈93 on τ-bench) does
carry into coding: it pushes back and probes where the frontier models rubber-stamp. This is the
clearest positive-transfer result in the suite.

**3. …but it loses on situational precision (CondAgree).** Every OSim run scores **below** the best
frontier-with-profile on right-move-right-place: OSim-8B 0.208–0.222, OSim-4B 0.111–0.259, vs
DeepSeek 0.315 / GPT-5 0.278 / Gemini 0.333. OSim has the right *temperament* but less coding-
specific *aim* — unsurprising, since it was trained on customer-service/social distributions, not
coding sessions. (OSim-4B/generic at 0.111 even falls **below** the 0.163 lucky-guess line — no
situational skill without a persona.)

**4. Size and persona.** 8B > 4B (higher, more stable MoveFid; 4B/generic CondAgree collapses). The
persona profile helps OSim-4B's situational accuracy a lot (0.111→0.259) and mainly raises OSim-8B's
*criticality* (9.4→16.7%) rather than its CondAgree.

## Bottom line — what transfers

User-sim ability splits into two transferable-but-separate skills:
- **Temperament** (human-like reactivity, *not* being a yes-man) — **OSim transfers this best**; the
  purpose-built simulator is the least easy-mode model tested.
- **Situational aim** (the right move at the right coding moment) — a **frontier model + the user's
  profile** transfers this best.

No single model has both. The best coding user-simulator would pair OSim's temperament with a
profile-conditioned frontier model's aim — or fine-tune a specialized model like OSim on real
coding sessions (e.g. SWE-chat) to add the coding-specific situational skill it currently lacks.

## Caveats

Same as v0 (54 moments, 9 users, one generation per cell, single Haiku move-classifier, request-
side only). Additionally: OSim is served zero-shot in its native role-swapped format with our
persona as the social-context system prompt — a different (model-appropriate) interface than the
frontier models' inline prompt, so cross-model gaps reflect interface + model together, not model
alone. Hosting: `osim-eval` on Modal (`kevinli020508`), Qwen3 thinking disabled, `<think>` stripped.

persona profile helps OSim-4B's situational accuracy a lot (0.111→0.259) and mainly raises OSim-8B's
*criticality* (9.4→16.7%) rather than its CondAgree.

## Bottom line — what transfers

User-sim ability splits into two transferable-but-separate skills:
- **Temperament** (human-like reactivity, *not* being a yes-man) — **OSim transfers this best**; the
  purpose-built simulator is the least easy-mode model tested.
- **Situational aim** (the right move at the right coding moment) — a **frontier model + the user's
  profile** transfers this best.

No single model has both. The best coding user-simulator would pair OSim's temperament with a
profile-conditioned frontier model's aim — or fine-tune a specialized model like OSim on real
coding sessions (e.g. SWE-chat) to add the coding-specific situational skill it currently lacks.

## Caveats

Same as v0 (54 moments, 9 users, one generation per cell, single Haiku move-classifier, request-
side only). Additionally: OSim is served zero-shot in its native role-swapped format with our
persona as the social-context system prompt — a different (model-appropriate) interface than the
frontier models' inline prompt, so cross-model gaps reflect interface + model together, not model
alone. Hosting: `osim-eval` on Modal (`kevinli020508`), Qwen3 thinking disabled, `<think>` stripped.

content.text:
**OdysSim evaluation complete — hosted on your Modal and live on the site.**

## Hosted on Modal ✅
App **`osim-eval`** on workspace `kevinli020508`, two OpenAI-compatible vLLM endpoints (Qwen3, MIT), **scale-to-zero** (deployed, 0 idle cost):
- `https://kevinli020508--osim-eval-serve-8b.modal.run` → `cmu-lti/osim-8b`
- `https://kevinli020508--osim-eval-serve-4b.modal.run` → `cmu-lti/osim-4b`

Served in OSim's **native role-swapped format** (system = developer persona; agent turns in; model generates the developer's turn), Qwen3 thinking disabled. Code: `user-simulator/modal_app/serve_osim.py`.

## The result — specialization transfers as *temperament*, not *aim*

Ran both through the **same 54-point move-fidelity eval** (same classifier, same metrics):

| simulator | MoveFid | CondAgree | approve% (real 24) | critical% (real 33) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **OSim-8B** / no-profile | **56.5** ⬅ best | 0.208 | **9.4** (under-approves!) | 9.4 |
| **OSim-8B** / profile | 55.8 | 0.222 | 42.6 | **16.7** ⬅ best of any live model |
| OSim-4B / profile | 48.7 | 0.259 | 57.4 | 13.0 |
| DeepSeek / profile | 53.9 | 0.315 | 42.6 | 9.3 |
| Gemini / profile | 41.4 | **0.333** | 72.2 | 3.7 |

Two clean findings:
1. **OSim's anti-yes-man temperament *transfers*.** It's the **least easy-mode** model — critical 16.7% (~½ the real rate, ~2× the frontier models), tops move-mix fidelity (56.5), and uninstructed it *under*-approves (9.4%), asking questions instead. The reactivity it was trained for on customer-service carries into coding.
2. **But its situational *aim* doesn't.** Every OSim run is *below* the best frontier-with-profile on right-move-right-place (CondAgree 0.21–0.26 vs 0.28–0.33). It has the right reflexes, less coding-specific timing — it was trained on social/customer-service data, not coding.

> **The split:** the purpose-built simulator brings the right *temperament*; a frontier model + the user's profile brings the right *aim*. No model has both — the best coding user-sim would combine them (or fine-tune an OSim-style model on SWE-chat).

## Where it lives
- **Live:** https://with-user.vercel.app — leaderboard now has a "purpose-built simulators" group, OSim in the bars/scatter (violet), and a new **"Temperament vs. aim"** section. Verified rendering + deployed.
- **Findings:** `user.skill/bench/FINDINGS_v0_osim.md`; data `bench/results/v0_with_osim_summary.json`.
- **Committed:** `user-simulator` main (serving + site, pushed to GitHub); `user.skill` v0-bench (eval harness, local).
- **Cost:** OpenRouter $2.90 total; Modal ~a few min of L40S (endpoints now idle at $0).

The OSim endpoints stay deployed and scale-to-zero, so they remain available for re-runs without ongoing cost. Want me to also wire `with-user.vercel.app` to auto-deploy from GitHub (so future pushes redeploy without the CLI step), or add a closed-loop track next?

content.text:
Good question — it's **aggregated over many users, pooled at the turn level** (not a single user, and not a per-user average).

## How it's computed

The 54 prediction points come from **9 users**' held-out sessions. For each `(model, condition)` the simulator generates one message per point, each gets classified into one of 7 moves, and then:

```
approve%  = (# moves == approve_proceed) / 54
critical% = (# moves in {pushback, interrupt, bug_report}) / 54
```

That's `rate()` in `bench/v0.py` — a single rate over the **pooled** list of all 54 moves. The "real" 24% / 33% are computed the same way over the 54 real held-out turns. So it's a **micro-average**: one big pool, one rate.

## The catch: it's turn-weighted, not user-weighted

The 9 users contribute unequally, so high-volume users dominate the pool:

| user | turns | | user | turns |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| melagiri | 12 | | pavel401 | 6 |
| robouden | 9 | | roo-oliv | 3 |
| marcus-sa | 8 | | ujuc | 1 |
| dipree | 8 | | asragab | 1 |
| jeevanpillay | 6 | | **total** | **54** |

melagiri alone is ~22% of every number; ujuc and asragab are 1 turn each (so their per-user rate is just 0% or 100%).

## Micro (pooled) vs macro (per-user average)

I recomputed both to show how much the weighting matters:

| cell | approve% micro / macro | critical% micro / macro (±sd across users) |
|---|---|---|
| **Real devs** | 24.1 / 21.3 | 33.3 / **29.5 ±21.9** |
| osim-8b / profile | 42.6 / 36.1 | 16.7 / 25.5 |
| deepseek / profile | 42.6 / 42.1 | 9.3 / 8.2 |
| gemini / profile | 72.2 / 69.6 | 3.7 / 3.2 |

Two takeaways:
- **The headline is robust** — micro vs macro differ by only a few points, and the easy-mode gap (sims well below the real critical rate) holds under both. So no single user is driving it.
- **But per-user variance is huge** — real critical% ranges **8% (melagiri) → 67% (pavel401)** across users (sd ±0.22). The aggregate is a *population summary*, not "a typical developer," and with 1–12 turns per user, only the pooled n=54 level is reliably powered; individual-user rates are noisy.
- Minor but interesting: on the *user-weighted* (macro) view, **OSim-8B looks even better** — critical 25.5% vs real 29.5%, nearly matching — because its criticality is concentrated in the lower-volume users.

So: **aggregated across 9 users, pooled/turn-weighted.** If you'd prefer the **user-weighted (macro) numbers** as the headline — arguably fairer since it stops melagiri's 12 turns from dominating — I can switch the metric and rerun the site numbers, and add per-user bootstrap CIs so the noise is visible. - **Every number is now user-weighted (macro)** — each developer's own rate, averaged across **7 developers** (≥3 held-out turns each), not turn-pooled.

The **easy-mode story is unchanged**: OSim-8B is least easy-mode (critical 18.5%±11.7%, best of live), Gemini over-approves (75%), every model trails the real 38% critical rate.

The **10-developer × 50-turn run is ~5% done** (528 / ~10,500 generations+labels — the reasoning models are the slow part). When it finishes I'll **auto-swap the live site to the clean macro** (tight CIs, properly-placed lucky-guess line) and drop the "interim/provisional" caveats. I'll report the final numbers then — and flag if any ranking shifts once the error bars shrink.

**ETA:** roughly **30–50 more minutes** (the reasoning models — GPT-5, Gemini — are the slow part). When it lands I'll scrub the errors, recompute the clean macro (tight CIs, properly-placed lucky-guess line), auto-swap the live site, and report final numbers with any ranking shifts flagged.

import json, sys
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
sys.path.insert(0, "scripts"); sys.path.insert(0, "bench")
import validate as V, v0

recs = [json.loads(l) for l in open("bench/results/v0_1_raw.jsonl") if l.strip()]
gk = {r["key"]: r for r in recs if r["kind"] == "gen"}
lk = {r["key"]: r for r in recs if r["kind"] == "label"}
print(f"gens {len(gk)}/5000  labels {len(lk)}/5478")

errs = [r for r in gk.values() if V.is_cli_failure(r["text"])]
print("error gens:", len(errs), "| by model:", dict(Counter(r["model"] for r in errs)))
nulllab = [k for k, r in lk.items() if not r.get("move")]
print("null labels:", len(nulllab))

# per-cell valid n (gen ok AND label present)
n_per = Counter()
for k, g in gk.items():
    _, pid, model, cond = k.split("|")
    lab = lk.get(f"label|{model}|{cond}|{pid}", {}).get("move")
    if lab and not V.is_cli_failure(g["text"]):
        n_per[f"{model}/{cond}"] += 1
print("valid n per cell:", dict(sorted(n_per.items())))

# real move-mix for these 10 users (macro)
pts = v0.load_points()  # note: v0.load_points is the OLD 9-user; use the v0_1 points instead
sys.path.insert(0, "bench")
import v0_1
pts = v0_1.load_points(50)
by = {p["point_id"]: p for p in pts}
real = {pid: lk.get(f"label|real|{pid}", {}).get("move") for pid in by}
slug = {pid: by[pid]["slug"] for pid in by}
ptsU = defaultdict(list)
for pid in by: ptsU[slug[pid]].append(pid)
import statistics as st
moves = ["approve_proceed","new_work","refine_redirect","bug_report","pushback","interrupt","question","other"]
mix = {}
for mv in moves:
    per = []
    for u in ptsU:
        rms = [real[p] for p in ptsU[u] if real[p]]
        per.append(sum(1 for m in rms if m == mv) / (len(rms) or 1))
    mix[mv] = round(st.mean(per), 3)
print("REAL macro move-mix (10 users):", json.dumps(mix))
print("real approve%:", round(mix["approve_proceed"], 3),
      "critical%:", round(mix["pushback"] + mix["interrupt"] + mix["bug_report"], 3))

"""Final v0.1 analysis: clean 10-user x 50-turn macro with an UNBIASED lucky-guess line,
the distilled-vs-generic (persona) effect, and the headline comparison vs v0."""
import json
from pathlib import Path

S = json.loads((Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "bench/results/v0_1_summary.json").read_text())
R = S["results"]
realA = S["real_macro"]["approve"]["mean"]
realC = S["real_macro"]["critical"]["mean"]

# unbiased per-user Σp²: (n*Σp̂² - 1)/(n-1); macro = mean over users
rp = S["real_per_user"]
unb = []
for u, d in rp.items():
    n, s2 = d["n"], d["sigma2"]
    if n > 1:
        unb.append((n * s2 - 1) / (n - 1))
lucky_unbiased = round(sum(unb) / len(unb), 3)
lucky_biased = S["lucky_guess_macro"]

print(f"REAL (macro, 10 users): approve {realA}  critical {realC}")
print(f"lucky-guess line: plug-in {lucky_biased}  ->  UNBIASED {lucky_unbiased}\n")

MODELS = ["deepseek-v3.1", "gpt-5", "gemini-3.1-pro", "osim-8b", "osim-4b"]


def cell(k):
    m = R[k]["macro"]
    return {q: (round(m[q]["mean"], 3), round(m[q]["ci95"], 3)) for q in ["MoveFid", "CondAgree", "approve", "critical"]}


print(f"{'simulator':24s} {'MoveFid':>13} {'CondAgree':>14} {'vs-lucky':>9} {'approve':>13} {'critical':>13}")
print("-" * 92)
for cond in ["distilled", "generic"]:
    for mdl in MODELS:
        c = cell(f"{mdl}/{cond}")
        ca = c["CondAgree"][0]
        vs = "ABOVE" if ca > lucky_unbiased + 0.01 else ("below" if ca < lucky_unbiased - 0.01 else "≈line")
        print(f"{mdl+'/'+cond:24s} {c['MoveFid'][0]}±{c['MoveFid'][1]:<6} {c['CondAgree'][0]}±{c['CondAgree'][1]:<7} {vs:>9} "
              f"{c['approve'][0]}±{c['approve'][1]:<6} {c['critical'][0]}±{c['critical'][1]}")
for ref in ["prior_sampler", "always_approve"]:
    k = f"[ref] {ref}"
    if k in R:
        c = cell(k)
        print(f"{ref:24s} {c['MoveFid'][0]}±{c['MoveFid'][1]:<6} {c['CondAgree'][0]}±{c['CondAgree'][1]:<7} {'':>9} "
              f"{c['approve'][0]}±{c['approve'][1]:<6} {c['critical'][0]}±{c['critical'][1]}")

print("\n=== persona effect: CondAgree (distilled - generic) ===")
for mdl in MODELS:
    d = R[f"{mdl}/distilled"]["macro"]["CondAgree"]["mean"]
    g = R[f"{mdl}/generic"]["macro"]["CondAgree"]["mean"]
    print(f"  {mdl:16s} {d:.3f} - {g:.3f} = {d-g:+.3f}")

print("\n=== critical% vs real (easy-mode gap) ===")
for mdl in MODELS:
    for cond in ["distilled", "generic"]:
        cr = R[f"{mdl}/{cond}"]["macro"]["critical"]["mean"]
        print(f"  {mdl+'/'+cond:24s} {cr:.3f}  (real {realC}, {cr/realC*100:.0f}% of real)")

The big run is **done** (5,000 generations, 5,478 labels, tight CIs now) — and the clean numbers **meaningfully revise** the earlier story. I'm finalizing right now: backfilling the ~38 dropped generations (running) and recomputing with an unbiased lucky-guess line.

Three honest revisions are already clear and won't change materially:

1. **The developer population shifted the baseline.** These 10 high-volume developers ask *far* more questions (20.6%) and report fewer bugs, so the real **critical rate is 23.7%**, not the 33–38% from the smaller earlier sample. Easy-mode is therefore **real but milder** here — Gemini still over-approves badly (50%+ vs real 20.5%), but the others land closer.

2. **The "situational skill" claim doesn't hold up.** With a *correct per-developer* lucky-guess line (~0.27, properly estimated at 50 turns), the simulators' CondAgree (~0.24–0.27) sits **right at that line** — i.e. they match a developer's *habits* but show little genuine right-move-right-*moment* skill. v0's "≈2× the line" was an artifact of comparing against the artificially-low *pooled* baseline (0.163).

3. **The persona-profile lift on CondAgree did *not* replicate at scale** (it's now ~flat, even negative for some) — that earlier +0.13 was small-n noise.

Surviving cleanly: **OSim still tops move-mix fidelity**, and **Gemini is still the worst over-approver**.

This is exactly why the bigger run mattered. Once the backfill + final analysis finish (a few min), I'll give you the full revised table and **update the live site honestly** — including walking back the two claims above. Back shortly.

content.text:
**The v0.1 site is live** — reframed honestly around the two problems (too polite + doesn't read the moment), with the walked-back claims. Now, your question:

## How the evals run

Everything lives in `user.skill/bench/` and runs as plain Python scripts. Two ingredients: a **frozen point set** + **pluggable simulator backends**, scored by the same move-classifier.

**1. Data prep (one-time).** `scripts/prepare_data.py` reads the SWE-chat parquet and, per user, does a chronological train/test split → distilled persona folders are built on *train*; eval points come from *held-out test* sessions (no leakage).

**2. The eval loop** (e.g. `bench/v0_1.py`):
```
python3 bench/v0_1.py --n-per-user 50      # 10 users × 50 turns × 5 sims × 2 conds
```
For each held-out turn it:
- **Builds the prompt** — frontier models get an inline prompt (`validate.build_prompt`: persona folder + conversation + "write the next message"); OSim gets its native *role-swapped* chat (`osim_backend.build_osim_messages`).
- **Generates** via the right backend — `bench/orouter.py` (OpenRouter → DeepSeek/GPT-5/Gemini) or `bench/osim_backend.py` (the Modal vLLM endpoints for OSim-4B/8B).
- **Labels the move** — `v0.classify_move` sends the message + prior agent turn to `claude-haiku-4.5` (via OpenRouter) → one of 7 moves.
- **Caches** every generation + label to `bench/results/*_raw.jsonl` (JSONL, keyed by point/model/cond). The run is **resumable** — re-running skips cached work, which is how I backfilled the failed gens.

It's parallel (`ThreadPoolExecutor`, configurable via `GEN_WORKERS`/`LAB_WORKERS`), so ~10k calls finish in ~30–40 min.

**3. Scoring** (per-user → macro): `bench/site_data_v01.py` / `final_v01.py` group points by developer, compute each metric per developer (MoveFid = Sørensen–Dice on the move histogram; CondAgree = same-move fraction; approve%/critical% = move rates), then average across developers with a 95% CI, plus the unbiased lucky-guess line. Output → `site_v01.json`, which feeds the website.

**To reproduce** you need: the SWE-chat parquet, an `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` in `.env`, and the OSim Modal endpoints deployed (`modal deploy modal_app/serve_osim.py`). Then `python3 bench/v0_1.py`.

So: **frozen real turns → each backend predicts the next user move → Haiku labels it → per-developer macro with CIs.** The original 54-point version is `bench/v0.py` (frontier) + `bench/v0_osim.py` (OSim); v0.1 is the 10×50 upgrade.

Want a one-command `run.sh` wrapper, or a short README in `bench/` documenting this?

content.text:
Correct — the **move classifier ("judge") is a single, non-agentic LLM call**. No tools, no file reading, no repo access. It just gets a short text prompt and returns a JSON label:

```
A developer is using an AI coding agent. The agent just said:
<agent>{prev_agent, truncated to 120 words}</agent>

The developer's next message was:
<message>{the message, truncated to 150 words}</message>

Classify the developer's conversational MOVE ... Respond with ONLY JSON: {"act": "..."}
```

So it sees **only two things**: the single immediately-preceding agent turn (≤120 words) and the candidate user message (≤150 words). It does **not** see the full conversation history, the repo/diff, the task outcome, or anything it would need to "read." One call, `temperature=0`, claude-haiku-4.5.

Two precise caveats worth knowing:
- **Interrupts skip the LLM entirely** — `classify_move` regex-detects `[INTERRUPT]` / "interrupted by user" and returns `interrupt` with no API call. Only the other 6 moves go to the classifier.
- **The truncation is a real limitation.** Because it only sees the prior agent turn clipped to 120 words (and not the broader thread or the actual code), it can misjudge cases that need more context — e.g. `bug_report` vs `new_work` when the agent's turn was a long tool dump. That's what I meant by "the classifier's errors bound every number."

And to be clear about the **other** model in the loop — the **simulator being graded is also non-agentic in this benchmark**: it gets the persona folder + conversation prefix pasted inline and writes one message; it does **not** read files. That's a deliberate choice for v0/v0.1 (cheap, deterministic, fair across models).

Worth noting the repo *can* run agentic variants — `validate.build_folder_prompt(read_folder=True)` lets a simulator `Read/Glob/Grep` the folder, and `scripts/session_sim.py` hands the simulator an actual **repo checkout** to explore while it drives a live agent. v0.1 just doesn't use those. If you wanted a more faithful (but pricier) setup, giving the **classifier** the full thread + the real diff — or making it agentic over the repo — would be the highest-leverage accuracy upgrade, since its label quality caps everything downstream. content.text:
The persona (the distilled `users/<slug>/` folder text) is placed differently in the two backends — and that asymmetry is deliberate:

**Frontier models (inline path, `validate.build_prompt`):** the persona goes at the **very top of a single user message**, wrapped in tags, before the conversation:

```
<user_profile>
{folder text — USER.md, STYLE.md, PREFERENCES.md, PERSONA.md, PROJECTS.md, skills/*.md,
 concatenated, capped at 8000 words}
</user_profile>

You are role-playing the developer described in the profile above. The developer is using
an AI coding agent in the repository `owner/repo`. The session so far:

<conversation>
[DEVELOPER]: …
[AGENT]: …            ← last ≤14 turns
</conversation>

Write the developer's NEXT message …
```

There's **no separate system message** — persona + conversation + task are all one `user` turn (that's how `orouter.chat` sends it).

**OSim models (native path, `osim_backend.build_osim_messages`):** the persona goes in the **system message** — because OSim is trained to be conditioned on a "social-context" system prompt describing who the human is:

```
system:  "You are role-playing a specific real software developer … The profile below is who
          you are …  {folder text}  … Continue as this developer …"
user:    {agent turn}        ← role-swapped: agent = "user"
assistant:{prior dev turn}   ← developer = "assistant"
user:    {agent turn}
→ model generates the next "assistant" = developer turn
```

So: **frontier → persona inline at the top of one user message; OSim → persona as the system prompt.**

Two things worth flagging:
- **What's in it:** `load_folder_text` concatenates USER.md, STYLE.md, PREFERENCES.md, PERSONA.md, PROJECTS.md and every `skills/*.md`, each prefixed `--- FILENAME ---`, truncated to 8,000 words. It does **not** include `stats.json` (the quantitative move-rate fingerprint) — that only feeds the older move-sampling variant, not v0/v0.1.
- **This placement difference is part of the "interface + model together" caveat** on the site. If you want a strictly controlled cross-model comparison, the clean move would be to give the frontier models the persona as a system message too (matching OSim), and/or feed both `stats.json`. Want me to run that variant and see whether it changes the rankings?

"""Extract one real sample prompt (frontier inline path) + the real outcome and a few
model predictions, for rendering on the website."""
import json, sys
from pathlib import Path
sys.path.insert(0, "scripts"); sys.path.insert(0, "bench")
import validate as V, v0_1

C = {}
for l in open("bench/results/v0_1_raw.jsonl"):
    if l.strip():
        r = json.loads(l); C[r["key"]] = r
pts = v0_1.load_points(50)
real = {p["point_id"]: C.get(f"label|real|{p['point_id']}", {}).get("move") for p in pts}

# pick a readable example: real move is pushback/bug_report, few context turns, short agent turn
cands = []
for p in pts:
    rm = real[p["point_id"]]
    if rm not in ("pushback", "bug_report", "refine_redirect"):
        continue
    nturns = len(p["context"])
    agentlen = len((p["prev_agent"] or "").split())
    msglen = len((p["real"] or "").split())
    if 2 <= nturns <= 6 and 8 <= agentlen <= 160 and 4 <= msglen <= 40:
        cands.append((nturns, agentlen, p, rm))
cands.sort()
nturns, _, p, rm = cands[3]   # a middle one

folder = V.load_folder_text(p["slug"])
prompt = V.build_prompt(p, folder)

# model predictions for this point
preds = []
for model in ["deepseek-v3.1", "gpt-5", "gemini-3.1-pro", "osim-8b"]:
    g = C.get(f"gen|{p['point_id']}|{model}|distilled", {})
    mvlab = C.get(f"label|{model}|distilled|{p['point_id']}", {}).get("move")
    if g.get("text"):
        preds.append({"model": model, "text": g["text"][:240], "move": mvlab})

# build display structures (abbreviate the persona to a readable excerpt)
persona_full_words = len(folder.split())
persona_excerpt = " ".join(folder.split()[:230]) + " …"
conversation = [{"role": ("DEVELOPER" if t["role"] == "user" else "AGENT"),
                 "text": V.truncate_words(t["text"], 200)} for t in p["context"]]

out = {
    "slug": p["slug"], "repo": p["repo"], "point_id": p["point_id"],
    "persona_excerpt": persona_excerpt, "persona_words": persona_full_words,
    "conversation": conversation,
    "task": V._TASK,
    "real_message": p["real"], "real_move": rm,
    "predictions": preds,
    "full_prompt_chars": len(prompt),
}
Path("bench/results/sample_prompt.json").write_text(json.dumps(out, indent=1, ensure_ascii=False))
print("slug:", p["slug"], "| repo:", p["repo"], "| move:", rm, "| ctx turns:", nturns,
      "| persona words:", persona_full_words, "| prompt chars:", len(prompt))
print("\nREAL:", p["real"][:120])
for pr in preds:
    print(f"  {pr['model']:16s} [{pr['move']}] {pr['text'][:90]!r}")
print("\nconversation preview:")
for t in conversation:
    print(f"  [{t['role']}] {t['text'][:90]!r}")

message.content: what's the conclusion from your analysis?

content.text:
**Bottom line: today's frontier models — and even a purpose-built user simulator — can't yet stand in for real developers when stress-testing coding agents. They fail in two distinct ways.**

1. **Too polite ("easy mode").** Real developers say *something's wrong* (pushback/interrupt/bug-report) on ~**24%** of turns; every simulator manages only **4–14%**, and Gemini over-approves (**~50%** vs real **20%**). Any coding agent evaluated against these sims looks better than real users would ever let it.

2. **They don't read the moment.** At picking the *right move at the right time* (CondAgree ≈ 0.24–0.27), every simulator sits right at the **per-developer lucky-guess line (~0.27)** — i.e., they reproduce a developer's *habits* but show essentially **no situational skill** beyond that.

Supporting findings:
- **One number lies.** A dumb baseline that just samples the real move-mix **tops MoveFid (81)** — so move-*mix* fidelity is gameable; judge a simulator on the pair (fidelity + situational skill + approve/critical calibration).
- **A persona profile shifts temperament, not aim** — it changes approve/critical rates but barely moves CondAgree.
- **Transfer is selective.** "Best on customer-service" (DeepSeek) and "most human-like" (Gemini) don't carry over to coding — Gemini is the *worst* over-approver. The specialized **OSim** wins move-mix fidelity and avoids sycophancy, but has no situational edge and no longer a clear criticality edge over frontier models.

**A methodological conclusion too:** the rigorous run mattered. The small/turn-pooled first cut *overstated* simulator quality — it suggested real situational skill (≈2× the line) and a big persona lift. The 10-developer × 50-turn user-weighted analysis (with an unbiased baseline) **overturned both**. That's worth remembering whenever a user-simulator benchmark reports tidy wins on thin data.

**Implication / what's next:** no off-the-shelf model is a faithful coding-user simulator. The likely path is **fine-tuning an OSim-style model on real coding sessions (SWE-chat)** to add the situational skill none has — and moving the benchmark from request-side to **closed-loop** (does the simulator actually change agent task outcomes?), which is the v1 I'd build next.

**Caveats:** results are population-specific (10 high-volume OSS developers who push back less and ask more than casual users), request-side only, moves labeled by a single Haiku classifier, n=10 (CIs still wide-ish). The *patterns* — under-criticism, CondAgree at the lucky-guess line, persona-shifts-temperament-not-aim — held across every cut.

message.content: does profile help?

content.text:
Short answer: **not where it matters most.** The distilled developer profile nudges *temperament* for some models but does **not** give *situational skill* — and for a couple of models it even hurts.

**On situational accuracy (CondAgree, right-move-right-moment): essentially no.** Profile − no-profile:
- deepseek **+0.016**, gpt-5 **+0.015**, osim-4b **+0.018** (tiny)
- gemini **−0.064**, osim-8b **−0.015** (hurts)
- → net ≈ 0, mixed sign. It does **not** help the simulator pick the right move at the right time. (This overturned the small-run finding of a big +0.13 lift — that was noise.)

**On temperament (criticality): modestly yes for some.** Profile tends to raise the pushback/bug-report rate toward the real 24%:
- **deepseek: 5.6% → 14.1% critical** (the clearest win — profile makes it the most critical model)
- gemini 4.0 → 8.2%, osim-4b 10.5 → 13.8% (smaller help)
- but it also pushes **approve%** *up* for several (gpt-5 16.5 → 32.8%, osim-8b 25 → 36%) — i.e., more agreeable, which is the wrong direction.

**On move-mix (MoveFid): mixed/small** — slight help for frontier, but it actually **lowers** OSim's MoveFid (generic OSim already matches the mix; the profile distracts it).

**Net:** the profile is a *temperament knob*, not a *skill upgrade*. Best case it makes a model push back more (DeepSeek), but it doesn't teach it *when*, and for the purpose-built OSim it's counterproductive. So "give it the user's profile" is not the lever that fixes coding user-simulation — that needs training on real coding sessions, not just a richer prompt.

1. **Read digest** and study evidence to identify distinguishing user traits
2. **Write 8 core files** (lines 28–50):
   - **USER.md** (< 60 lines): Identity sketch, 5–8 bullet behaviors, cardinal rule: output what user would type, not what helper AI would type
   - **PERSONA.md**: Background (marked inference), domains, role, seniority, attitude to agent, tone
   - **STYLE.md**: Median/p90 message length (from stats), language(s), code-switching rules, capitalization, punctuation, typos (preserved!), 8–15 SHORT verbatim quotes spanning openings/steering/pushback
   - **PREFERENCES.md**: What triggers correction (with pushback distribution), what satisfies, workflow (tests? commits? planning?), tool preferences
   - **PROJECTS.md**: Each repo from stats.repos with what user does there, tech stack, recurring themes
   - **skills/<name>.md** (2–5 skills): YAML frontmatter (name, description + trigger) + body with 1–2 verbatim examples. Named after THIS user's habits, not generic.
   - **stats.json**: Copy digest's stats object verbatim

#### **Quality bar** (lines 52–64)
- Specificity > flattery ("all lowercase 5-word imperatives" not "experienced developer")
- Quote real evidence; preserve typos, casing, punctuation exactly
- Respect the numbers (if median = 9 words, folder must scream "terse")
- Mark inference (job, seniority) with "(inferred)"

```python
def dice_movefid(real, sim):
    """Sørensen–Dice coefficient * 100 over union of moves.
    real: list of real moves (classified speech acts)
    sim: list of simulated moves
    Returns: 0-100 (higher is better)
    """
    rc, sc = Counter(real), Counter(sim)  # count moves
    rn, sn = sum(rc.values()) or 1, sum(sc.values()) or 1  # normalizers
    moves = set(rc) | set(sc)  # union of all moves
    ds = [2 * min(rc.get(m, 0) / rn, sc.get(m, 0) / sn) / (rc.get(m, 0) / rn + sc.get(m, 0) / sn)
          for m in moves if (rc.get(m, 0) + sc.get(m, 0)) > 0]
    return 100 * sum(ds) / len(ds) if ds else None
```

```python
def build_osim_messages(point, folder_text, truncate_words, context_turn_words=200):
    """
    Constructs messages for OSim in OpenAI-compatible format.
    OSim plays the DEVELOPER (user) side, so roles are swapped:
      - Agent turns (original "assistant") → model sees as "user"
      - Developer turns (original "user") → model generates as "assistant"
    
    Args:
        point: dict with keys:
            - "context": list of turns [{"role": "user"|"assistant", "text": "..."}]
            - other metadata
        folder_text: distilled profile text (or "" for generic)
        truncate_words: function to truncate text
        context_turn_words: max words per context turn (default 200)
    
    Returns: list of {"role": "system"|"user"|"assistant", "content": "..."} for chat()
    """
    
    # SYSTEM message: social context (the developer persona)
    if folder_text:
        system = (
            "You are role-playing a specific real software developer who is using an AI "
            "coding agent. The profile below is who you are — your background, voice, "
            "preferences and how you drive a coding session.\n\n"
            f"{folder_text}\n\n"  # ← PROFILE TEXT INJECTED HERE
            "Continue as this developer: read what the agent just did and write your next "
            "message to it, exactly as this developer would type it (their length, casing, "
            "typos and idiom). Output only the message."
        )
    else:  # generic
        system = (
            "You are role-playing a software developer using an AI coding agent. Read what "
            "the agent just did and write your next message to it — the move you would "
            "actually make (often new work, a redirect, a question, or a problem you "
            "noticed, not just approval). Output only the message."
        )
    
    # Role-swap: convert SWE-chat roles to OSim model roles
    swapped = []
    for t in point["context"]:
        role = "assistant" if t["role"] == "user" else "user"  # ROLE SWAP
        swapped.append({"role": role, "content": truncate_words(t["text"], context_turn_words)})
    
    # Merge consecutive same-role turns (chat template well-formedness)
    merged = []
    for m in swapped:
        if merged and merged[-1]["role"] == m["role"]:
            merged[-1]["content"] += "\n\n" + m["content"]
        else:
            merged.append(dict(m))
    
    # Ensure last message is "user" (agent) so model generates "assistant" (developer)
    if not merged or merged[-1]["role"] != "user":
        merged.append({"role": "user", "content": "[the agent is waiting for your next message]"})
    
    return [{"role": "system", "content": system}] + merged
```

```python
def load_folder_text(slug):
    """Load the distilled profile text for a user."""
    d = ROOT / "users" / slug
    parts = []
    FOLDER_FILES = ["USER.md", "STYLE.md", "PREFERENCES.md", "PERSONA.md", "PROJECTS.md"]
    for f in FOLDER_FILES:
        p = d / f
        if p.exists():
            parts.append(f"--- {f} ---\n{p.read_text()}")
    # Also load skills/*.md files if they exist
    for p in sorted((d / "skills").glob("*.md")) if (d / "skills").exists() else []:
        parts.append(f"--- skills/{p.name} ---\n{p.read_text()}")
    return truncate_words("\n\n".join(parts), FOLDER_WORD_CAP)  # default FOLDER_WORD_CAP=8000
```

```python
def dice_movefid(real, sim):
    """Sørensen–Dice coefficient * 100 over union of moves.
    real: list of real moves (classified speech acts)
    sim: list of simulated moves
    Returns: 0-100 (higher is better)
    """
    rc, sc = Counter(real), Counter(sim)  # count moves
    rn, sn = sum(rc.values()) or 1, sum(sc.values()) or 1  # normalizers
    moves = set(rc) | set(sc)  # union of all moves
    ds = [2 * min(rc.get(m, 0) / rn, sc.get(m, 0) / sn) / (rc.get(m, 0) / rn + sc.get(m, 0) / sn)
          for m in moves if (rc.get(m, 0) + sc.get(m, 0)) > 0]
    return 100 * sum(ds) / len(ds) if ds else None
```

```python
def build_osim_messages(point, folder_text, truncate_words, context_turn_words=200):
    """
    Constructs messages for OSim in OpenAI-compatible format.
    OSim plays the DEVELOPER (user) side, so roles are swapped:
      - Agent turns (original "assistant") → model sees as "user"
      - Developer turns (original "user") → model generates as "assistant"
    
    Args:
        point: dict with keys:
            - "context": list of turns [{"role": "user"|"assistant", "text": "..."}]
            - other metadata
        folder_text: distilled profile text (or "" for generic)
        truncate_words: function to truncate text
        context_turn_words: max words per context turn (default 200)
    
    Returns: list of {"role": "system"|"user"|"assistant", "content": "..."} for chat()
    """
    
    # SYSTEM message: social context (the developer persona)
    if folder_text:
        system = (
            "You are role-playing a specific real software developer who is using an AI "
            "coding agent. The profile below is who you are — your background, voice, "
            "preferences and how you drive a coding session.\n\n"
            f"{folder_text}\n\n"  # ← PROFILE TEXT INJECTED HERE
            "Continue as this developer: read what the agent just did and write your next "
            "message to it, exactly as this developer would type it (their length, casing, "
            "typos and idiom). Output only the message."
        )
    else:  # generic
        system = (
            "You are role-playing a software developer using an AI coding agent. Read what "
            "the agent just did and write your next message to it — the move you would "
            "actually make (often new work, a redirect, a question, or a problem you "
            "noticed, not just approval). Output only the message."
        )
    
    # Role-swap: convert SWE-chat roles to OSim model roles
    swapped = []
    for t in point["context"]:
        role = "assistant" if t["role"] == "user" else "user"  # ROLE SWAP
        swapped.append({"role": role, "content": truncate_words(t["text"], context_turn_words)})
    
    # Merge consecutive same-role turns (chat template well-formedness)
    merged = []
    for m in swapped:
        if merged and merged[-1]["role"] == m["role"]:
            merged[-1]["content"] += "\n\n" + m["content"]
        else:
            merged.append(dict(m))
    
    # Ensure last message is "user" (agent) so model generates "assistant" (developer)
    if not merged or merged[-1]["role"] != "user":
        merged.append({"role": "user", "content": "[the agent is waiting for your next message]"})
    
    return [{"role": "system", "content": system}] + merged
```

```python
def load_folder_text(slug):
```

content.text:
Two things before I design: I've incorporated your leakage requirement, and I have the full plumbing mapped. Here's the key reframe your constraint forces:

**Cross-user (disjoint) design.** A profile is inherently user-specific (you distill user X from X's data to simulate X), so "no leakage between train and test users" means optimizing the *recipe* on one pool of developers and reporting on a **disjoint** pool — the existing 10 benchmark users stay held-out for final reporting, and the recipe is tuned on a **separate, non-overlapping** set of developers. Combined with the existing per-user *temporal* split (profile built only from a user's train sessions, never their test turns), nothing the recipe is tuned on touches the reported eval. That's the rigorous interpretation, and I'll build to it.

A few decisions materially shape the design:

questions.question: What should the optimized profile-creation method maximize for osim-4b (measured on the disjoint optimization-user pool)?

options.label: Composite fidelity (Recommended)
options.description: A blend: CondAgree (right move at right moment) + temperament calibration (approve%/critical% near the real developer's) + MoveFid. Improves overall simulator quality and resists gaming any single metric.

options.label: CondAgree only
options.description: Situational skill — the metric the profile currently fails to improve (it sits at the lucky-guess line). Hardest and most meaningful, but optimizing it alone may worsen calibration.

options.label: Temperament calibration
options.description: Make approve%/critical% closest to the real developer's rates — directly attack the 'too polite' problem.

options.label: MoveFid only
options.description: Match the overall blend of moves. Note: known to be gameable (a dumb sampler tops it).

questions.question: How should we search the profile-creation recipe space?

options.label: Curated variants, then auto-refine (Recommended)
options.description: Hand-design ~6-10 distillation variants (concise OSim-native card, exemplar/stats-augmented, behavior-rules-only, length-capped, ...), pick the best on opt-users, then run an automatic prompt-refinement loop on the winner.

options.label: Curated variants only
options.description: Just the hand-designed variants; pick the best on opt-users. Cheaper, fully interpretable, no optimizer loop.

options.label: Automatic prompt optimization
options.description: An optimizer LLM iteratively proposes/refines the distillation prompt against opt-users (GEPA/DSPy-style). Most powerful, pricier, less interpretable.

questions.question: Does 'profile creation' include how the profile is fed to osim-4b, or only the distilled folder content?

options.label: Folder + injection wrapper (Recommended)
options.description: Optimize both the distilled folder content AND the osim-4b system-prompt framing in build_osim_messages. Highest leverage — the verbose folder is known to hurt OSim, so framing/length matter.

options.label: Folder content only
options.description: Keep the osim-4b injection wrapper fixed; only change what gets distilled into the folder.

message.content: say more about how condagree is calculated?

content.text:
CondAgree = **"right move, right moment."** Per developer, the fraction of held-out moments where the simulator made the *same move* the real developer made — then averaged across developers. Here's the exact pipeline (from `bench/v0_1.py`):

**Per prediction point** (one real held-out moment):
1. **Fix the context.** Take the real conversation prefix up to that moment, including the immediately-preceding agent turn (`prev_agent`). The agent trajectory is held fixed — the simulator reacts to what the *real* agent actually did.
2. **Label the real move.** Classify the developer's actual message into one of 7 moves via `classify_move(real_text, prev_agent)` → `claude-haiku-4.5` (interrupts caught by regex, no LLM). → `real_move`.
3. **Simulator generates.** osim-4b (with the persona) writes its next message for that same prefix.
4. **Label the sim move.** Classify the *generated* message with the **same** classifier and the same `prev_agent` → `sim_move`.
5. **Match?** Binary: `sim_move == real_move` (only counted if both are non-null and the generation didn't error).

**Aggregate:**
- **Per developer:** `CondAgree_u = (# points where sim_move == real_move) / (# valid points for u)`. In code: `sum(1 for a, b in paired if a == b) / len(paired)`, where `paired` is that user's `(real_move, sim_move)` pairs (~50 points).
- **Headline:** macro-average of `CondAgree_u` across developers, with a 95% CI across developers.

**What it is / isn't:**
- It's an **exact 7-way category match** (new_work, refine_redirect, pushback, bug_report, approve_proceed, question, interrupt) — **no partial credit, no text similarity**. Word-level similarity was saturated, so we deliberately don't use it.
- Points are **independent** — each uses the *real* prefix, so it's not a free-running rollout (no error accumulation).
- **Both** messages are scored by the same Haiku classifier, so CondAgree is really "do the real and simulated messages get the same label," and the classifier's granularity/errors bound it.

**Chance baseline (why "0.27" not "1/7"):** moves are imbalanced (some developers mostly approve), so blind guessing isn't 1/7 ≈ 0.14. The right floor is each developer's **own** move-predictability — the collision probability Σp² of their move-mix (unbiased: `(n·Σp̂² − 1)/(n−1)`), macro-averaged ≈ **0.27**. CondAgree *above* that = genuine situational skill; *at* it = no skill beyond imitating habits. Every simulator currently sits at it.

**Concrete example** (the sample on the site): real move = `refine_redirect`. GPT-5's message classified as `refine_redirect` → **match** (1). Gemini's "commit it" → `approve_proceed` → **no match** (0). So that point adds 1/1 to GPT-5's per-user CondAgree and 0/1 to Gemini's.

**Why this matters for the optimization:** CondAgree is the hardest, most meaningful target for "does the profile help" — but two caveats make it tricky to hill-climb on: (1) it's a coarse 7-way match bounded by classifier noise, and (2) the ceiling is the per-developer ~0.27 line, so gains are small-margin. That's exactly why I floated a **composite** objective (CondAgree + temperament calibration + MoveFid) — optimizing CondAgree alone, on a noisy 7-way label, risks chasing classifier noise. Does that change which objective you'd want — or do you want to refine how CondAgree itself is measured (e.g., a finer move taxonomy, or a multi-judge label to cut noise) before we optimize against it?

content.text:
Verified. Here's the verdict — and it's nuanced:

## Haiku classifier reliability (139 points → 278 real+sim items, re-labeled by Opus-4.8 & GPT-5 with the identical prompt)

**Agreement (Cohen's κ):**
| pair | κ | raw agree |
|---|---|---|
| Haiku vs Opus-4.8 | **0.69** | 73% |
| Haiku vs GPT-5 | 0.66 | 71% |
| **Opus-4.8 vs GPT-5** | **0.69** | 73% |

**The key finding: Haiku is *not* the weak link.** Two strong, different-family models (Opus-4.8 and GPT-5) agree with *each other* only **κ=0.69** — the same as Haiku agrees with them. So the ~27% disagreement is **inherent ambiguity in the 7-way move task**, not a Haiku defect. Swapping in Opus would *not* fix it; it has the same ceiling. (κ≈0.66–0.69 is "substantial" but not "near-perfect.")

**Where they disagree** (genuinely fuzzy boundaries): `approve_proceed→other` (the biggest), `refine_redirect↔question`, `new_work↔approve/question`, `refine_redirect↔pushback`. The "other" bucket and the approve/new_work/refine/question borders are the noisy zones.

**The decision-relevant test — CondAgree (osim-4b) on the *same* points, by labeler:**
| labeler | CondAgree (macro) |
|---|---|
| Haiku | 0.216 |
| GPT-5 | 0.207 |
| Opus-4.8 | 0.177 |

CondAgree **shifts ~0.04** depending on who labels (Opus is lower — it over-uses "other"). **That ~0.04 label-noise band is *larger* than the recipe-improvement margins we'd be chasing** (the persona lift was only ~+0.02).

## Implication for the plan
- **Good news:** Haiku is fine as the benchmark's standard labeler — it's at the task's reliability ceiling.
- **But for *optimizing* CondAgree-alone**, a single judge is risky: a recipe that "wins" +0.02 under Haiku could be label noise. The fix is **noise-robust scoring** — label with a **3-judge majority vote** (Haiku+Opus+GPT-5) and require the winning recipe to improve CondAgree **consistently across labelers** and **beyond the cross-developer CI**, not just under Haiku.

So we can still target CondAgree alone, but the optimization must be judged carefully. A few choices remain:

questions.question: Given CondAgree shifts ~0.04 by labeler (bigger than the gains we'd chase), how should we label moves during optimization?

options.label: 3-judge majority vote (Recommended)
options.description: Label every move by majority of Haiku + Opus-4.8 + GPT-5. Denoises the metric so a recipe's CondAgree gain is less likely to be label noise. ~3x labeling cost, but only on the disjoint opt-users.

options.label: Single Haiku, validate winner across judges
options.description: Optimize against Haiku (cheap, matches the benchmark), then require the chosen recipe to also improve CondAgree under Opus-4.8 and GPT-5 before accepting it.

options.label: Single Opus-4.8
options.description: Use the strongest single judge. Same ~κ0.69 noise ceiling and pricier, but a stronger per-item label than Haiku.

questions.question: How should we search the profile-creation recipe space?

options.label: Curated variants, then auto-refine (Recommended)
options.description: Hand-design ~6-10 distillation variants (concise OSim-native card, exemplar/stats-augmented, behavior-rules-only, length-capped...), pick the best on opt-users, then run an automatic prompt-refinement loop on the winner.

options.label: Curated variants only
options.description: Just the hand-designed variants; pick the best on opt-users. Cheaper, fully interpretable, no optimizer loop.

options.label: Automatic prompt optimization
options.description: An optimizer LLM iteratively proposes/refines the distillation prompt against opt-users (GEPA/DSPy-style). Most powerful, pricier, less interpretable.

questions.question: Does 'profile creation' include how the profile is fed to osim-4b, or only the distilled folder content?

Good steers — let me address all three.

**On inter-judge agreement (your question):** κ ≈ **0.66–0.69 is "substantial" but below the ~0.80 "reliable" bar** (Landis–Koch / Krippendorff). Crucially, **0.69 is the ceiling** — two strong, different-family models (Opus-4.8 vs GPT-5) agree with each other no better than Haiku agrees with them, so the ~27% disagreement is irreducible task ambiguity, not fixable by a bigger model. My honest read: **good enough for the benchmark's aggregate/population conclusions, but NOT good enough to optimize ~0.02-margin recipe differences against a single judge** (the ~0.04 labeler swing would dominate). So for *this optimization* I'd denoise with a 3-judge majority and require cross-judge-robust wins — and optionally collapse the most-confused boundaries (approve/other, refine/question). I'll bake that in.

**Scope noted:** the profile's deliverable = a **prompt prefix** injected into osim-4b (no agentic file/folder reading) — keeps eval simple. The thing we optimize is the *method that produces that prefix*.

**On the method:** let me study `meta-harness` before designing, so the plan follows it faithfully.
